title: Takaichi’s Approval Shield: Prospects for Her Second Year in Office
gist: Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi retains an unusually strong 'approval shield' resembling Abe and Koizumi that deters LDP rivals, but softening ratings, a fiscally divisive consumption-tax cut, a September reshuffle, and an Upper House minority test her second year; foreign and defense policy show strong continuity, with Japan hitting 2 percent GDP defense spending two years early.

themes.theme: The approval shield and LDP standing

insights.claim: Takaichi's cabinet approval fell from 64.4 percent at the start of her administration to 50.2 percent in the latest Kyodo poll, but the approval-disapproval gap remains unusually wide with no crossover in sight, resembling Abe's strong second-administration opening.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A durable approval buffer lowers near-term Japanese political-leadership risk, supporting policy continuity that markets can price.
insights.quote: no approval-disapproval crossover yet in sight

insights.claim: Takaichi's 'prime minister premium'—cabinet approval minus support for the leading ruling party—is large by recent standards and comparable to the reformist Koizumi era, indicating her strength rests partly on personal appeal rather than LDP partisanship.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Personal-appeal-driven support gives her latitude to push difficult policy and deters intra-party challenges.
insights.quote: comparable to the level seen under the popular reformist Junichiro Koizumi in the early 2000s

insights.claim: Takaichi's support increasingly rests on the passive 'no suitable alternative' reason, which rose from 18.1 percent last October to 30.5 percent by August, now her single largest source of support.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Rising passive support signals her shield is softening in quality, a leading indicator of vulnerability if a credible rival emerges.
insights.quote: making it the single largest reason for support

insights.claim: Takaichi lacks her own factional base; the 80-percent-of-lawmakers National Power Research Group is a broad policy forum rather than a reliable support faction, leaving her cohesion uncertain.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Absence of a dedicated faction is a structural weakness that could surface if her approval shield erodes.
insights.quote: Takaichi lacks a factional base of her own

insights.claim: The Diet session that ended in July passed all government bills—only the fourth 100 percent passage rate in the postwar era—but required an eight-day extension amid opposition walkouts and coalition friction with the Japan Innovation Party.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A historic legislative win masks coalition management strain that will recur in the fall session.
insights.quote: marking only the fourth time in the postwar era that the government achieved a 100 percent passage rate

insights.claim: A gap between public priorities and the government's 64-bill agenda contributed to softening approval: 92 percent wanted anti-inflation measures prioritized in October 2025, but by August 64 percent disapproved of the government's inflation response.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Voter frustration on cost-of-living is the main threat to Takaichi's shield and the pressure behind her tax-cut pivot.
insights.quote: The government had advanced a crowded legislative agenda of 64 bills that, on its face, had little direct connection to everyday economic concerns.

insights.claim: Takaichi instructed the LDP to prepare legislation cutting the consumption tax on food and beverages from 8 percent to 1 percent for two years starting April 2027, paired with cash benefits, despite a projected revenue shortfall of roughly ¥5 trillion ($31.7 billion) annually.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A material fiscal loosening tied to social-security funding, relevant to Japanese fiscal sustainability and JGB/yen watchers.
insights.quote: the proposed cut is expected to create a revenue shortfall of roughly ¥5 trillion ($31.7 billion) annually

insights.claim: NHK polling found 49 percent support Takaichi's tax-cut proposal versus 39 percent opposed, but 67 percent expressed concern about its fiscal impact, and the DPFP opposes the cut.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Fiscal-credibility concerns and Upper House arithmetic make passage and market reception uncertain.
insights.quote: 67 percent expressing concern about the fiscal impact

insights.claim: The LDP-JIP coalition lacks an Upper House majority, forcing Takaichi to seek issue-by-issue opposition cooperation on the consumption tax cut and the carried-over Lower House seat reduction bill.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Upper House minority is the practical brake on Takaichi's agenda, shaping what actually becomes law.
insights.quote: the LDP-JIP ruling coalition lacks a majority in the Upper House
insights.locator: Outlook for Domestic Politics and Foreign Policy

insights.claim: Japan reached its 2 percent of GDP defense spending target two years ahead of the 2022 strategy's schedule, and will revise its three strategic documents by year-end with an updated threat assessment addressing drone warfare.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Confirms sustained Japanese defense-budget expansion and a fresh procurement cycle, a tailwind for defense-industrial and drone exposure.
insights.quote: reaching the 2 percent of GDP target two years ahead of the original schedule
insights.locator: Outlook for Domestic Politics and Foreign Policy

insights.claim: Takaichi benefits from broad LDP alignment on U.S.-Japan alliance priorities including increased defense spending, defense industrial base coordination, and greater emphasis on economic security, signaling continuity in Japan's external engagement.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Policy continuity on the alliance and economic security reduces geopolitical uncertainty for U.S.-Japan-linked positioning.
insights.locator: Outlook for Domestic Politics and Foreign Policy

insights.claim: A September cabinet and LDP leadership reshuffle looms, with attention on how Takaichi handles the Aso faction whose support was instrumental to her leadership victory and whether she adjusts her economic team amid yen depreciation and 2025 U.S.-Japan trade deal investment commitments.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The reshuffle and economic-team composition are near-term signals for Japan's fiscal and FX policy direction.
insights.locator: Outlook for Domestic Politics and Foreign Policy
